blurb: Why AI runs on graphics chips: thousands of small cores, the memory bottleneck, smaller numbers, and wiring thousands together.

steps.h: The CPU: a few brilliant workers
steps.p: A computer's main chip, the CPU, has a handful of very powerful cores. Each finishes complicated, step-by-step jobs quickly.
steps.analogy: A few professors: brilliant, but there are only a few of them.

steps.h: The GPU: thousands of simple workers
steps.p: A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that all do the same kind of sum at once. Built to colour millions of screen pixels for video games.
steps.analogy: A stadium of students each doing one simple sum at the same moment.

right.title: GPU
points: Great at many identical sums at once

steps.h: AI is mostly one kind of sum
steps.p: Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplication: huge grids of numbers multiplied together — millions of independent multiply-and-add steps. Perfect for a GPU.
GPU cores run in groups of 32 (called warps) that all do the same instruction together. If some need to do something different, the others wait.
GPUs weren't designed for AI. Researchers realised around 2009–2012 that gaming chips happened to be perfect for neural networks.

cards.q: Which operation makes up most of the computing in training a language model?
cards.why: Matrix multiplication. Almost every layer multiplies big grids of numbers. It's simple and repetitive — exactly what GPUs are built for.

cards.statement: GPUs were originally designed for AI.
cards.why: False. They were built for video-game graphics. AI researchers borrowed them because the maths is so similar.

cards.title: AlexNet, the 2012 network that started the deep-learning boom, was trained on two gaming GPUs.
cards.detail: Alex Krizhevsky used two NVIDIA GTX 580 cards with 3 GB of memory each, splitting the network across them because it didn't fit on one.

cards.q: On NVIDIA GPUs, cores run in lockstep groups called warps. How many threads are in a warp?
cards.why: 32. All 32 do the same instruction together, which is efficient when they all have the same work.

cards.statement: If threads in the same warp need to do different things, the warp slows down.
cards.why: True. The group runs one path, then the other, with some threads idle each time. GPU code avoids this where it can.

steps.p: A GPU can do maths much faster than it can fetch the numbers from memory. Often the cores sit waiting for data.
steps.analogy: A super-fast chef who spends most of the time waiting for ingredients to arrive.

steps.p: Tiny, very fast memory sits right inside the chip; bigger, slower memory (HBM) sits beside it.

items: HBM beside the chip: big, slower

steps.p: To write each new word, the GPU must read every one of the model's billions of numbers — and does only a couple of sums with each. Reading is the bottleneck.
Serving many users together lets one read of the numbers produce words for all of them.
So clever GPU code focuses on reusing data while it's close by, rather than fetching it again.

cards.q: HBM, the memory beside every AI chip, stands for…
cards.why: High Bandwidth Memory. Stacks of memory chips right next to the GPU, built to move data as fast as possible.

cards.q: Why is writing text for one user mostly limited by memory, not maths?
options: Every number must be read for each new word but is used for only a couple of sums
The GPU runs out of maths
cards.why: Lots of reading, little maths. With one user, each fetched number does very little work before the next must be fetched.

cards.statement: Batching many users' requests together makes text generation more efficient per user.
cards.why: True. One read of the numbers serves everyone in the batch, so the expensive part is shared.

cards.title: An NVIDIA H100 can read its entire 80 GB of memory roughly 40 times per second.
cards.detail: It moves about 3.35 TB per second. A model filling that memory can be read about 40 times a second — capping one user at about 40 tokens per second.

options: Memory built right inside the chip
cards.hint: Look at the ladder in step 2.
cards.why: On-chip memory. It's closest to the cores, so it's fastest — but tiny and expensive.

cards.title: Doing more maths with fewer bits

steps.p: Since 2017, NVIDIA GPUs include tensor cores — circuits that multiply small grids of numbers in one go, far faster than normal cores.
A number can be stored with 32 bits (very precise), 16, 8 or even 4. Fewer bits = less memory, faster maths, but less precision.
steps.analogy: Like measuring in millimetres vs centimetres vs metres: coarser units are quicker but less exact.

steps.p: Each format splits its bits between range (how big or small a number can be) and detail. BF16 keeps a wide range with less detail — and suits AI well.
In training, tiny updates would round to zero in a low-precision number. So a precise master copy is kept, and the fast maths uses the smaller format.
Training moved from 32-bit to 16-bit, and frontier labs now train largely in 8-bit — roughly doubling speed each step.

cards.q: BF16 became the default training format over FP16 mainly because it…
options: Keeps a wide range of sizes, so numbers rarely become too big or too small
cards.why: Wide range. BF16 matches 32-bit's range with less detail. Training rarely needs the detail but often hits extreme sizes.

cards.statement: NVIDIA introduced tensor cores with its V100 GPU in 2017.
cards.why: True. The Volta-generation V100 was the first, and every generation since has made them faster.

cards.q: Why keep a precise master copy of the parameters during low-precision training?
options: Tiny updates would round to zero if added straight to low-precision numbers
For backup in case of fire
cards.why: Tiny updates survive. Adding 0.0001 to 1.0 in a coarse format can round back to 1.0 — and the model stops learning.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V3 was trained largely in 8-bit numbers (FP8), one of the first top-scale models to do so.
cards.detail: Its 2024 report describes careful scaling tricks to keep accuracy. Along with other efficiencies, it helped make training unusually cheap.

cards.statement: Smaller number formats only help when running models; training always needs 32-bit.
cards.why: False. Training in 16-bit has been standard for years, and 8-bit training is now used at the frontier.

steps.p: A typical AI server holds 8 GPUs linked by NVLink — direct connections far faster than normal computer wiring.
Servers connect through very fast networks, so thousands of GPUs can work on one model.

items: Many racks linked by fast network

steps.p: After each step, GPUs average their results so every copy of the model stays the same. This step is called all-reduce.
steps.analogy: Everyone in a group project sharing their findings so all notes match.

steps.p: NVIDIA's lead isn't just chips: it's CUDA, the software almost all AI code is written for, plus its networking.
One top GPU draws up to about 700 watts — like a microwave. An 8-GPU server draws over 10 kilowatts.

cards.q: In training, what does the all-reduce step do?
options: Averages results across GPUs so every model copy stays identical
cards.why: Keeps copies in sync. Each GPU learned from different data; averaging combines those lessons.

cards.q: Analysts often say NVIDIA's strongest advantage isn't its chips but…
options: CUDA and the software built on it
cards.why: CUDA. Years of tools, libraries and know-how make switching to rival chips hard.

cards.statement: Google trains its Gemini models mainly on NVIDIA GPUs.
cards.why: False. Google uses its own TPU chips — one of the few big labs not depending on NVIDIA for training.

cards.title: A single H100 GPU can draw up to 700 watts — about as much as a microwave.
cards.detail: An 8-GPU server draws over 10 kilowatts. That's why AI data centers are planned around power and cooling.

cards.title: Estimate GPU memory in your head
cards.body: Running a model takes about 2 bytes per parameter at 16-bit. So a 7B model needs about 14 GB; a 70B model about 140 GB.
cards.challenge: Work out how much memory a 13-billion-parameter model needs at 16-bit, then at 4-bit.
